subject: Introduction to Mechanical Engineering
title: Mechanics of Materials and Structures
sourceBasis: Wickert & Lewis, An Introduction to Mechanical Engineering, 2016

questions.a: The internal resisting force per unit area developed in a material under external loading.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of stress?
questions.a: Pascal (Pa), equal to N/m².
The deformation produced per unit original dimension of a body.
Yes. It is a ratio of two lengths.
Normal stress produced when a member is subjected to a pulling load.
Normal stress produced when a member is subjected to a pushing or compressive load.
Stress acting tangentially to an area and tending to cause relative sliding between adjacent layers.

questions.q: Write the basic normal-stress relation for uniform axial loading.
questions.a: σ = P/A, where P is axial load and A is the loaded cross-sectional area.
The property by which a material tends to regain its original shape and dimensions after removal of the load, within its elastic range.
The ability of a material to undergo permanent deformation without rupture after the elastic range is exceeded.

questions.q: What is strength of a material?
questions.a: Its ability to resist applied loads without failure.
The ability of a material to absorb energy and deform plastically before fracture.
The resistance of a material to localized permanent deformation such as indentation or scratching.
Loading in which the applied force acts along the longitudinal axis of a member.

questions.q: What type of stress is primarily produced by a concentric axial tensile load?
questions.a: Tensile normal stress.

questions.q: What type of stress is primarily produced by a concentric axial compressive load?
questions.a: Compressive normal stress.
Deformation of a member caused by a bending moment, generally producing curvature and a distribution of normal stresses across the section.
Twisting of a member caused by an applied torque or twisting moment.
A structural member primarily designed to resist transverse loads and bending effects.
A structure made of interconnected members arranged generally in triangular units to carry loads mainly through axial forces.
An individual component of a structure that carries and transfers applied loads.
The change in shape or dimensions of a body caused by applied loading or other effects.
Stress acting perpendicular to a cross-sectional area.

questions.q: What is the main difference between normal stress and shear stress?
questions.a: Normal stress acts perpendicular to the area, whereas shear stress acts tangentially to the area.

questions.q: Why is toughness important in engineering materials?
questions.a: It indicates the ability to absorb energy before fracture and is important where impact or sudden loading may occur.

questions.q: Why is hardness important for machine components?
questions.a: It helps a surface resist wear, indentation and localized deformation.

questions.q: What happens to an elastic material when the load is removed within its elastic range?
questions.a: It tends to return to its original dimensions.

questions.q: What happens when a material is loaded beyond its elastic range?
questions.a: Permanent or plastic deformation can remain after unloading.
The determination of basic structural responses such as member forces, reactions and stresses under specified loading and support conditions.

questions.q: Why are support conditions important in structural analysis?
questions.a: They determine the restraints and reactions that influence the structural response.
The turning effect of a force or load about a reference point or section, associated with bending of a member.
The twisting moment applied about the longitudinal axis of a member.

questions.q: Which loading produces twisting of a shaft?
questions.a: Torque or twisting moment.

questions.q: What is the purpose of structural design?
questions.a: To proportion and select structural members so that they safely and adequately perform their intended function under specified loads and conditions.

questions.q: Why must both strength and deformation be considered in design?
questions.a: A component must resist failure while also keeping deformation within acceptable limits for proper function.
A characteristic of a material that describes its response or performance under specified conditions or loading.

questions.q: Name the three basic stress types listed in the ME25C03 Unit II syllabus.
questions.a: Tensile, compressive and shear stresses.

questions.q: Name the three mechanical properties specifically listed with strength in the Unit II syllabus.
questions.a: Toughness and hardness are listed along with strength.

questions.q: Which two deformation modes are specifically introduced in Unit II besides axial loading?
questions.a: Bending and torsion.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of torque in the SI system?
questions.a: N·m (newton-metre).

questions.q: What is the SI unit of bending moment?
questions.a: N·m (newton-metre).

questions.q: What is the engineering purpose of a truss or beam demonstration in Unit II?
questions.a: To illustrate basic structural analysis and response to loading using a simple structural model.
